old_entry.title: Nintendo 3DS
old_entry.subtitle: Depth without a pair of glasses
old_entry.summary: The familiar two-screen handheld gained a stereoscopic upper display, a Circle Pad and a new relationship with movement and space.
body: Nintendo 3DS retained a recognisable arrangement: two screens, physical buttons and a touchscreen below. Its upper display changed what that familiar object could show. Stereoscopic depth was visible without wearing special glasses, and a slider let players adjust the effect. The first Japanese systems arrived on 26 February 2011.

A Circle Pad added analogue movement beside the D-pad. Cameras, motion sensing and a gyroscope gave software further ways to respond to the world around the screen. Older DS and DSi game cards remained usable, so the new machine carried an existing library into a different set of possibilities. Not every game had to use every feature; choosing which inputs mattered remained a design decision.

The hardware's identity also appeared through later colours and special editions. Nintendo's black-and-gold Zelda 25 th Anniversary bundle reached Europe on 25 November 2011, with a Hyrule emblem and Ocarina of Time 3D. That edition belongs to the same first-year 3DS body, but its November release should not replace the February date of the original system. The larger XL and later New Nintendo 3DS designs are separate revisions.

Nintendo 3DS launched in Japan in February 2011. Its upper screen could display stereoscopic images without special glasses, and a physical slider let the player adjust the effect or turn it off. Below it, the touch screen continued an interaction familiar from the Nintendo DS.

The Circle Pad, motion sensor and gyro sensor expanded the available inputs. The system also supported existing Nintendo DS software. That compatibility connected the new device to an established collection, while developers could decide how the newer controls and display suited their own games.

StreetPass exchanged data with nearby 3DS systems in sleep mode; SpotPass could receive material through supported wireless connections. Nintendo also included cameras for stereoscopic photographs and cards for augmented-reality play. The hardware proposed activities between game sessions, not only more elaborate pictures during them.

old_entry.title: Marvel vs. Capcom 3: Fate of Two Worlds
old_entry.subtitle: Three on Three Between Comics and Arcades
old_entry.summary: Three-character teams turn Marvel and Capcom fighters into combinations of active attacks, assists and timed resources.
body: Marvel vs. Capcom 3: Fate of Two Worlds brought its crossover to PlayStation 3 and Xbox 360 in 2011. A team contains three fighters drawn from Marvel comics and Capcom games. The selection makes unlikely combinations possible before a round begins: recognisable characters become parts of a team the player has assembled.

Calling an assist brings a teammate briefly into the fight. That extra attack can cover an approach or extend a combination, while changing the active fighter changes the available moves. Learning a team involves the relationships between its members, not only the commands of a favourite character.

X-Factor offers a limited burst of enhanced ability, giving a struggling team a way to turn the match. It adds a decision about when to spend a powerful resource. The spectacle of beams and airborne combinations rests on these choices about order, support and timing.

old_entry.title: Homefront
old_entry.subtitle: The Familiar Becomes Strange Before the Fighting Even Begins
old_entry.summary: Homefront places its resistance fighters in a fictional occupied United States. Familiar streets, civilian spaces and military spectacle frame a shooter built around the uneasy distance between home and battlefield.
body: David Votypka described Homefront's visual principle with a simple idea: take familiar places and make them alien. Residential neighborhoods, schools, gas stations and sports fields are not replaced by science-fiction settings, but bent by military occupation and scarcity. This choice shifts narrative weight onto the environment. The player recognizes the objects and original functions of these places, and therefore perceives more clearly what has changed. Kaos Studios thus seeks a contrast different from that of the typical military shooter, where the war zone is often already separated from everyday life. In Homefront, war enters directly into what should be domestic. Level design becomes a form of storytelling: moving through a space means reading traces of what it was before the occupation.

In Homefront's multiplayer, Battle Points do not work like permanent experience. David Votypka explained that they are earned during a match through kills, assists and objectives, then spent immediately on ammunition, rocket launchers, EMP grenades, drones, air strikes or vehicles. The distinction matters because score stops being only a measure of performance and becomes a tactical currency. Spending immediately can solve a local problem; saving points instead allows the player to respawn with more expensive equipment. Vehicles are also handled through purchases at respawn, avoiding a rush toward a tank that has just appeared on the map. The system therefore links individual behavior to the scale of the battle, making equipment and support emerge directly from decisions taken during that specific match.

THQ presents Homefront as an occupation of the United States in 2027 and credits John Milius with a role in shaping the story, alongside consultation from a former CIA agent to develop a sequence of events capable of supporting the premise. The work is not meant to turn fiction into prediction, but to give the world continuity before the player enters the first mission. A political and economic timeline establishes how the country reached the crisis and allows environments to show consequences instead of constantly explaining causes. The method reveals a production priority: the shooter needs a context defined enough to make propaganda, occupation, resistance and civilian life coherent. Storytelling therefore does not coincide only with scripted scenes; it begins with the construction of the world that makes those scenes plausible within the fiction.

The method reveals a production priority: the shooter needs a context defined enough to make propaganda, occupation, resistance and civilian life coherent. Storytelling therefore does not coincide only with scripted scenes; it begins with the construction of the world that makes those scenes plausible within the fiction.

body: Portal 2 is a 2011 first person puzzle-platform game developed by Valve for Windows, macOS, Linux, PlayStation 3, and Xbox 360. The retail versions and PlayStation 3 and Xbox 360 versions were distributed by Electronic Arts. A port for the Nintendo Switch was released as part of the Portal: Companion Collection in June 2022.

Like the original Portal (2007), players solve puzzles by placing portals and teleporting between them. Portal 2 adds features including excursion funnels (called tractor beams in files), lasers, light bridges, and paint-like gels that alter player movement or allow portals to be placed on any surface. In the single-player campaign, players control Chell, who navigates the dilapidated Aperture Science Enrichment Center during its reconstruction by the supercomputer GLaDOS (Ellen McLain); new characters include robot Wheatley (Stephen Merchant) and Aperture founder Cave Johnson (J. K. Simmons). In the new cooperative mode, players solve puzzles together as robots Atlas and P-Body (both voiced by Dee Bradley Baker). Jonathan Coulton and the National produced songs for the game.

Valve announced Portal 2 in March 2010, and promoted it with alternate reality games including the Potato Sack, a collaboration with several independent game developers. After release, Valve released downloadable content and a simplified map editor to allow players to create and share levels.

Portal 2 received critical acclaim for its gameplay, balanced learning curve, pacing, dark humor, writing, and acting. Like its predecessor, it has been described as one of the greatest video games ever made by numerous publications and critics.

old_entry.summary: Ridge Racer 3D is a 2011 racing video game developed and published by Namco Bandai Games for the Nintendo 3DS.
body: Ridge Racer 3D is a 2011 racing video game developed and published by Namco Bandai Games for the Nintendo 3DS. It is the first Ridge Racer series title on a Nintendo platform since Ridge Racer DS (2004) and, as usual for the series, revolves around cars racing around high speed tracks while drifting. The game received positive reviews and was a commercial success.
The game introduces a Drift button, specially designed for beginners to the Ridge Racer series and allows them to drift easily using one button press.

There are two main gameplay types: Single Player and Versus. Versus is a multi-player mode which allows the ability to play against other players via a wireless connection in Standard Race, One-Make Race and Team Battle by either hosting or joining a race using Nintendo 3DS local play.

Other minor gameplay types include: Records (allowing the player to view their records achieved in Single Player and check local rankings based on records acquired from friends or via StreetPass), AV player (allowing to watch replays of past races while listening to music of choice), Options, and Garage (allowing to view and modify cars the player has acquired).
Grand Prix: Competing in a series of races in order to win new cars and nitrous kits or to make them available for purchase.
Time Attack: Racing around a track as fast as possible for 3 laps in order to achieve the fastest time or beat a ghost.
Namco Bandai had announced the creation of a Ridge Racer for Nintendo's upcoming system at E3 2010. The game was designed to take advantage of the device screen's 3D stereo view.

old_entry.summary: Terraria ( tə-RAIR-ee-ə) is a 2011 action-adventure video game developed and published by Re-Logic.
body: Terraria ( tə-RAIR-ee-ə) is a 2011 action-adventure video game developed and published by Re-Logic. As a sandbox game, Terraria has no set goals. After creating the player character and choosing the game's difficulty, the player is placed in a two-dimensional, procedurally generated world where they explore, fight enemies, gather resources, and craft equipment. Players beat bosses, a tougher variety of enemies, to gain access to more items, resources, and equipment. By completing select goals, players receive access to non-player characters (NPCs) who sell items and offer services, such as healing and fishing quests. Terraria can be played alone or with others, and features support for modding.

Andrew Spinks commenced development in January 2011; he was assisted by a team of game testers and designers. As of 2025, Terraria is developed by eleven members of Re-Logic. Initially released in May 2011 on the Steam digital store, Terraria has received continuous content updates that have considerably changed it from its first version. The game was originally set to end development in 2012, but it resumed in 2013.

new_entry.title: Terraria
new_entry.summary: Terraria is a 2011 action-adventure video game developed and published by Re-Logic.
body: Terraria is a 2011 action-adventure video game developed and published by Re-Logic. As a sandbox game, Terraria has no set goals. After creating the player character and choosing the game's difficulty, the player is placed in a two-dimensional, procedurally generated world where they explore, fight enemies, gather resources, and craft equipment. Players beat bosses, a tougher variety of enemies, to gain access to more items, resources, and equipment. By completing select goals, players receive access to non-player characters (NPCs) who sell items and offer services, such as healing and fishing quests. Terraria can be played alone or with others, and features support for modding.

Andrew Spinks commenced development in January 2011; he was assisted by a team of game testers and designers. As of 2025, Terraria is developed by eleven members of Re-Logic. Initially released in May 2011 on the Steam digital store, Terraria has received continuous content updates that have considerably changed it from its first version. The game was originally set to end development in 2012, but it resumed in 2013.

old_entry.title: Deus Ex: Human Revolution
old_entry.summary: Deus Ex: Human Revolution is an action role-playing game developed by Eidos-Montréal and published by Square Enix.
body: Deus Ex: Human Revolution is an action role-playing game developed by Eidos-Montréal and published by Square Enix. The game is a prequel to the original Deus Ex (2000) and the third installment in the Deus Ex series. The gameplay combines first-person shooter, stealth, and role-playing elements. It features exploration and combat in environments connected to multiple city-based hubs, in addition to quests that grant experience and allow customization of the main character's abilities with items called Praxis Kits. Set in the year 2027, players control Adam Jensen, a security officer for Sarif Industries, a company which develops controversial artificial organs dubbed "augmentations". After an attack on Sarif, Jensen undergoes extensive augmentation and investigates the shadowy organization behind the attack. The story explores themes of transhumanism and the growing power of megacorporations and their impact on social class. It also uses the series' cyberpunk setting and conspiracy theory motif.

Development of Human Revolution began in 2007 with a small team within the fledgling Eidos-Montréal studio after failed attempts to create a sequel at original developer Ion Storm following Deus Ex: Invisible War (2003). The two key influences were the myth of Icarus, a thematic element carried over from Deus Ex, and the artwork and ideas of the Renaissance, which influenced the story, graphics, and music while combining with the series' typical cyberpunk elements. The open-ended gameplay was tricky for the team to achieve; the boss battles were outsourced to another developer due to time constraints. The music, composed by Michael McCann, focused on ambience and three-layered compositions over character themes and overt melodies. Human Revolution was announced in 2007, soon after its beginning development. Its title and release window were announced in 2010.

Human Revolution was released for PlayStation 3, Windows, and Xbox 360 in August 2011. The game received critical acclaim for its player-driven plot, gameplay, and freedom of choice in the story and character customization. The major criticisms went to its boss fights and technical problems. The director's cut was praised for its revamped gameplay. By November 2011, the original version had sold 2.18 million units. After release, a downloadable episode, The Missing Link, was developed, featuring gameplay improvements. A director's cut, featuring further improvements and additional content, was released in October 2013 for the original platforms and Wii U. The game was followed up with a spin-off, The Fall in 2013, and a direct sequel, Mankind Divided in 2016.

body: The Witcher 2: Assassins of Kings‍ is a 2011 action role-playing game developed by CD Projekt Red, based on The Witcher series of fantasy novels authored by Andrzej Sapkowski. It is a sequel to the 2007 game, The Witcher and the second main installment in The Witcher's video game series. It was released for Windows, Xbox 360, OS X, and Linux.

The player directs the actions of Geralt of Rivia, a monster hunter known as a Witcher. The fantasy world in which his adventures take place owes much to Polish history and Slavic mythology. The game was both a critical and commercial success, selling over eight million copies by September 2014. The third installment in the series, The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt, was released in 2015. A fourth installment, The Witcher IV, is planned for release in 2028.

new_entry.summary: The Witcher 2: Assassins of Kings is a 2011 action role-playing game developed by CD Projekt Red, based on Andrzej Sapkowski's fantasy novels.
body: The Witcher 2: Assassins of Kings is a 2011 action role-playing game developed by CD Projekt Red, based on The Witcher series of fantasy novels authored by Andrzej Sapkowski. It is a sequel to the 2007 game, The Witcher and the second main installment in The Witcher's video game series. It was released for Windows, Xbox 360, OS X, and Linux.

The gameplay of The Witcher 2 is a marked departure from that of its predecessor. Combat, for instance, is more complex, with additions in the form of abilities to lay traps and aim and throw ranged weapons. The protagonist, Geralt, has an improved offensive and defensive arsenal, with a range of melee and ranged weapons, armor, bombs, traps, and secondary weapons such as hatchets and shovels.

Upgrades are divided into four paths: an initial training path, which includes generalized upgrades for core abilities and must be invested in before the other paths can be accessed; swordsmanship, which improves Geralt's sword-fighting abilities; alchemy, which includes perks such as reducing the negative effects of potions; and magic, which improves Witcher Signs.

Geralt's profession is hunting monsters, but his journey also passes through struggles for power in the Northern Kingdoms. The developer describes a nonlinear story in which decisions can have serious consequences. The adventure contains different story paths and multiple endings, making the player's choices part of how events unfold rather than merely a way to select equipment. Trading settlements, mining towns, castles and fortresses provide the setting for these encounters and conflicts.

old_entry.title: Bastion
old_entry.summary: Bastion is a 2011 action role-playing video game developed by independent developer Supergiant Games and originally published by Warner Bros.
body: Bastion is a 2011 action role-playing video game developed by independent developer Supergiant Games and originally published by Warner Bros. Interactive Entertainment. In the game, the player controls "the Kid" as he moves through floating, fantasy-themed environments and fights enemies of various types. It features a dynamic voiceover from a narrator (Logan Cunningham), and is presented as a two-dimensional game with an isometric camera and a hand-painted art style. Bastion's story follows the Kid as he collects special shards of rock to power a structure, the Bastion, in the wake of an apocalyptic Calamity.

The game was built over the course of two years by a team of seven people split between San Jose and New York City. They introduced the game at the September 2010 Penny Arcade Expo, and it went on to be nominated for awards at the 2011 Independent Games Festival and win awards at the Electronic Entertainment Expo prior to release. Bastion was published in July 2011 for Xbox 360 via Xbox Live Arcade, and in August 2011 through digital distribution for Microsoft Windows on Steam. Supergiant Games made it available as a browser game for Google Chrome in December 2011. It was released for Mac OS X and iOS in 2012, for PlayStation 4 and PlayStation Vita in 2015, for Xbox One in 2016, and Nintendo Switch in 2018. Bastion's soundtrack was produced and composed by Darren Korb, and a soundtrack album was made available for sale in August 2011.

During 2011, the game sold more than 500,000 copies, 200,000 of which were for the Xbox Live Arcade. It sold over three million copies across all platforms by January 2015. The game was widely praised by reviewers, primarily for its story, art direction, narration, and music. Opinions were mixed on the depth of the gameplay, though the variety of options in the combat system was praised. Bastion has won many nominations and awards since its release, including several for best downloadable game and best music, from review outlets such as IGN and Game Informer as well as from the Spike Video Game Awards, the Game Developers Conference, and the Academy of Interactive Arts & Sciences.

editorial_features.title: Two voices inside Bastion
editorial_features.summary: What do the soundtrack credits reveal beyond the name of a composer?
body: Bastion's official soundtrack credits Darren Korb with writing, producing and recording its music, but they identify vocal performances separately. Ashley Barrett sings Build That Wall, while Korb sings Mother, I'm Here. The distinction lets a listener follow people as well as melodies. A composer's name on an album does not mean that the same person performed every sound it contains. Starting with the individual credits gives the songs a clearer human setting and makes room for the different work involved in writing a piece, recording it and singing it.

The album credits bring Barrett and Korb together on Setting Sail, Coming Home. Other entries distinguish lyrics by Greg Kasavin and performances by Logan Cunningham. These details resist a shorthand in which one celebrated name absorbs everyone else's contribution. They also suggest a useful listening route: move between a solo vocal and the shared performance, paying attention to how the voices occupy the arrangement. That comparison is an invitation to hear the recording, not a claim about an undocumented studio session. No song lyric needs to be reproduced to make its authorship visible.

Supergiant's description of Bastion places a reactive narrator beside its action role-playing structure and the work of building a refuge. That spoken presence belongs to the same game as the songs, but it has a different job. One responds to an unfolding action; the album presents fixed recordings with their own performers and credits. Keeping the forms distinct helps an exhibit discuss voice without reducing it to a single category. A visitor can compare narration, a sung phrase and an instrumental passage while asking what each one makes available to the player.

In March 2012, Greg Kasavin announced guitar and piano arrangements of four Bastion songs after requests from listeners. These sheets offered another way to encounter the music: through a playable arrangement rather than only a recording. The date belongs to that later publication, not to the game's original launch. Nor does a freely offered arrangement automatically grant permission to redistribute every page or performance. The announcement is useful evidence of a specific response to an audience, connecting a game's soundtrack to people who wanted to make the music with their own hands.

new_entry.title: Bastion
new_entry.summary: Bastion is a 2011 action role-playing video game developed by independent developer Supergiant Games and originally published by Warner Bros.
body: Bastion is a 2011 action role-playing video game developed by independent developer Supergiant Games and originally published by Warner Bros. Interactive Entertainment. In the game, the player controls "the Kid" as he moves through floating, fantasy-themed environments and fights enemies of various types. It features a dynamic voiceover from a narrator (Logan Cunningham), and is presented as a two-dimensional game with an isometric camera and a hand-painted art style. Bastion's story follows the Kid as he collects special shards of rock to power a structure, the Bastion, in the wake of an apocalyptic Calamity.

The game was built over the course of two years by a team of seven people split between San Jose and New York City. They introduced the game at the September 2010 Penny Arcade Expo, and it went on to be nominated for awards at the 2011 Independent Games Festival and win awards at the Electronic Entertainment Expo prior to release. Bastion was published in July 2011 for Xbox 360 via Xbox Live Arcade, and in August 2011 through digital distribution for Microsoft Windows on Steam. Supergiant Games made it available as a browser game for Google Chrome in December 2011. It was released for Mac OS X and iOS in 2012, for PlayStation 4 and PlayStation Vita in 2015, for Xbox One in 2016, and Nintendo Switch in 2018. Bastion's soundtrack was produced and composed by Darren Korb, and a soundtrack album was made available for sale in August 2011.

During 2011, the game sold more than 500,000 copies, 200,000 of which were for the Xbox Live Arcade. It sold over three million copies across all platforms by January 2015. The game was widely praised by reviewers, primarily for its story, art direction, narration, and music. Opinions were mixed on the depth of the gameplay, though the variety of options in the combat system was praised. Bastion has won many nominations and awards since its release, including several for best downloadable game and best music, from review outlets such as IGN and Game Informer as well as from the Spike Video Game Awards, the Game Developers Conference, and the Academy of Interactive Arts & Sciences.

editorial_features.title: Darren Korb and Ashley Barrett
editorial_features.summary: Darren Korb's compositions, Ashley Barrett's singing and Logan Cunningham's narration give Bastion several distinct voices.
body: Darren Korb wrote, produced and recorded Bastion's original soundtrack, released on 5 August 2011. Its credits also identify the singers of individual songs. Ashley Barrett performs Build That Wall, while Korb sings Mother, I'm Here. Composition, production and performance are different parts of the same recording: Korb's role as the album's composer does not mean that every voice on it is his. Barrett's performance gives one of the soundtrack's central songs its own identifiable voice.

Barrett and Korb sing together on Setting Sail, Coming Home, the ending theme. The album therefore includes both their individual performances and a shared song. Its credits also name Greg Kasavin as the lyricist of Get Used to It and Logan Cunningham as its vocalist. Following those credits reveals a collaboration rather than a soundtrack made by one person alone. Listening to the solo songs and then the ending offers a way to hear the different voices within the same musical world.

Logan Cunningham is also the voice of Bastion's narrator, Rucks. Supergiant describes narration that reacts to the player's actions as the Kid travels through the world and rebuilds the refuge. The spoken narration and the songs belong to the same game, but work differently: the narrator responds to events during play, while the soundtrack album presents fixed recordings. Cunningham's spoken presence therefore forms another part of Bastion's vocal identity alongside Barrett's and Korb's singing.

On 15 March 2012, Greg Kasavin announced official guitar and piano arrangements of four Bastion songs. Supergiant explained that listeners had requested tabs and sheet music since the game's debut, and offered the collection free of charge as thanks for their support. These arrangements provided a different way to engage with the soundtrack: playing the songs rather than only hearing the recordings. The publication followed the original 2011 release and connected the game's music with an audience who wanted to perform it.

editorial_before_2011_plain_language_rev.title: Two voices inside Bastion
editorial_before_2011_plain_language_rev.summary: What do the soundtrack credits reveal beyond the name of a composer?
body: Bastion's official soundtrack credits Darren Korb with writing, producing and recording its music, but they identify vocal performances separately. Ashley Barrett sings Build That Wall, while Korb sings Mother, I'm Here. The distinction lets a listener follow people as well as melodies. A composer's name on an album does not mean that the same person performed every sound it contains. Starting with the individual credits gives the songs a clearer human setting and makes room for the different work involved in writing a piece, recording it and singing it.

The album credits bring Barrett and Korb together on Setting Sail, Coming Home. Other entries distinguish lyrics by Greg Kasavin and performances by Logan Cunningham. These details resist a shorthand in which one celebrated name absorbs everyone else's contribution. They also suggest a useful listening route: move between a solo vocal and the shared performance, paying attention to how the voices occupy the arrangement. That comparison is an invitation to hear the recording, not a claim about an undocumented studio session. No song lyric needs to be reproduced to make its authorship visible.

Supergiant's description of Bastion places a reactive narrator beside its action role-playing structure and the work of building a refuge. That spoken presence belongs to the same game as the songs, but it has a different job. One responds to an unfolding action; the album presents fixed recordings with their own performers and credits. Keeping the forms distinct helps an exhibit discuss voice without reducing it to a single category. A visitor can compare narration, a sung phrase and an instrumental passage while asking what each one makes available to the player.

In March 2012, Greg Kasavin announced guitar and piano arrangements of four Bastion songs after requests from listeners. These sheets offered another way to encounter the music: through a playable arrangement rather than only a recording. The date belongs to that later publication, not to the game's original launch. Nor does a freely offered arrangement automatically grant permission to redistribute every page or performance. The announcement is useful evidence of a specific response to an audience, connecting a game's soundtrack to people who wanted to make the music with their own hands.
